# 2011 Sawyerville–Eoline tornado

## Lead

The **2011 Sawyerville–Eoline tornado** was a long‑tracked, strong tornado that occurred in central Alabama during the afternoon and early evening of April 27, 2011, as part of the 2011 Super Outbreak of tornadoes across the southeastern United States. The tornado was rated EF3 on the Enhanced Fujita scale by the National Weather Service (NWS), with an estimated maximum wind speed of about 145 mph (233 km/h), a maximum path width of roughly 1 mile (1,760 yd), and an overall path length of 72.13 miles (116.1 km) across Greene, Hale, and Bibb counties. Along its track from near Tishabee in far southwest Greene County through the communities of Sawyerville, Harper Hill, and Eoline to near Marvel in northeastern Bibb County, the tornado caused severe damage to hundreds of structures, including the destruction of numerous mobile homes, single‑family houses, a church, and the Eoline Fire Department, and it downed thousands of trees. NWS Birmingham’s event summary and outbreak table attribute 7 fatalities and 50 injuries to the full Sawyerville–Eoline tornado track, while the NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) Storm Events database segment for the Hale County portion lists 6 direct deaths and 40 direct injuries, reflecting NCEI’s practice of reporting county‑based segments rather than whole‑track totals. 

## Background and synoptic setting

The Sawyerville–Eoline tornado formed during a large and deadly tornado outbreak that affected the southeastern United States from April 25 to 28, 2011, commonly referred to as the 2011 Super Outbreak. A NOAA service assessment reported that the broader outbreak produced 368 confirmed tornadoes, including 224 on April 27 alone, with four EF5, eleven EF4, and twenty‑one EF3 tornadoes, causing approximately 324 fatalities, more than 3,100 injuries, and about 12 billion USD in damage. 

Within this multi‑day outbreak, April 27, 2011, featured several waves of severe thunderstorms and tornadoes that moved across Alabama from before sunrise into the late evening. NOAA’s GeoPlatform hub describes multiple rounds of tornado‑ and wind‑damage‑producing storms crossing the state over nearly 18 hours, while the NCEI episode narrative notes that this sequence broke the state record for the number of tornadoes in a single day and characterizes it as the most significant tornado outbreak in Alabama’s history. 

NWS Birmingham’s historic outbreak summary divides the day into multiple waves of storms and indicates that the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado occurred during the most intense afternoon and evening phase of tornado activity in central Alabama. In statewide summaries of the April 25–28 period, NOAA and NWS note that the combined tornado pathlengths reached about 3,200 miles, the greatest of any documented U.S. tornado outbreak and roughly 600 miles longer than the total pathlength in the 1974 Super Outbreak, underscoring the exceptional scale of the environment that produced the Sawyerville–Eoline event. 

## Meteorological history

According to the NWS Birmingham event review, the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado touched down in far southwest Greene County, Alabama, near the Tombigbee River just west of the community of Tishabee along County Road 69 near Head Drive during the late afternoon or early evening of April 27, 2011. The NWS outbreak summary provides start coordinates of 32.6152°N, 88.0543°W and an approximate start time of 5:30 p.m. Central Daylight Time. From its point of origin, the tornado moved generally east‑northeast across Greene, Hale, and Bibb counties before dissipating east of West Blocton in northeastern Bibb County. 

Survey information from NWS Birmingham describes the tornado as a long‑tracked, strong tornado rated EF3 on the Enhanced Fujita scale, with an estimated maximum wind speed of 145 mph. The same sources give a total damage path length of 72.13 miles and a maximum path width of 1,760 yards (about 1 mile) for the track across Greene, Hale, and Bibb counties, and they list 7 fatalities and 50 injuries associated with the event. Tornado Talk’s overview of the April 25–28 outbreak classifies the Sawyerville–Eoline event as one of the twenty‑one EF3 tornadoes confirmed during the Super Outbreak. 

The NWS narrative notes that the tornado’s intensity evolved along its path. In Greene County, damage initially corresponded to EF1 intensity but increased to EF2 as the tornado progressed, damaging at least four mobile homes, three outbuildings, and two churches, and uprooting or snapping numerous trees. As the tornado crossed the Black Warrior River into Hale County, it intensified further, reaching EF3 strength near and just north of Sawyerville and maintaining EF3 intensity in and near Eoline, before weakening to EF2 south of West Blocton and gradually dissipating near Marvel. 

NCEI’s Storm Events database provides a county‑specific entry (Event ID 314742) for the Hale County segment of the tornado, listing an EF3 rating, a segment path length of 25.18 miles, a maximum width of 1,760 yards, and a start and end time from 4:43 p.m. to 5:20 p.m. local time, with the segment beginning about 4.92 miles west of Sawyerville and ending about 3.64 miles east‑southeast of Phipps. In contrast, the NWS Birmingham outbreak table aggregates the full multi‑county track under a single “Sawyerville–Eoline (Greene, Hale and Bibb Counties)” entry, which explains the longer 72.13‑mile pathlength and higher casualty totals listed in that source. 

## Damage and impacts

Damage surveys and official databases indicate that the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado caused significant structural damage along much of its path, particularly in and near the communities of Sawyerville, Harper Hill, and Eoline. The NWS Birmingham report states that hundreds of structures were damaged or destroyed, including numerous mobile homes and single‑family residences, one church, and the Eoline Fire Department, and that thousands of trees were downed along the track from Greene County into Bibb County. 

In Greene County, the tornado’s early stages produced EF1 to EF2 damage. NWS Birmingham documents that near Tishabee, the tornado damaged or destroyed at least four mobile homes, three outbuildings, and two churches and caused extensive tree damage, with two minor injuries reported in this county. This initial damage reflects the intensifying phase of the tornado before it crossed the Black Warrior River toward Hale County. 

The most severe damage in Hale County occurred as the tornado crossed Alabama Route 14 just north of Sawyerville and continued through rural areas toward Harper Hill and Ingram. Both the NWS survey and the NCEI event narrative state that the tornado intensified to EF3 strength near Route 14, with estimated winds of 145 mph, and that it caused extensive structural damage along County Roads 18 and 21, Alabama Highway 69 south of Harper Hill, and County Road 29 east of Ingram. Numerous mobile homes and single‑family houses, along with one church, were damaged or destroyed in these locations, and thousands of trees were knocked down as the tornado moved toward the Talladega National Forest and the Bibb County line. 

In the Eoline area of Bibb County, the tornado again produced EF3‑level damage. NWS Birmingham reports that numerous mobile homes and single‑family homes sustained minor to major damage, that about a dozen such dwellings were destroyed, and that both the Eoline Fire Department and another business were destroyed. The same report notes that one fatality occurred in a vehicle near the fire station and that at least ten other injuries were recorded in this portion of the track. ArcGIS StoryMaps material similarly emphasizes that the most intense damage occurred near Sawyerville, Harper Hill, and Eoline, where extensive structural damage included complete destruction of some buildings. 

As the tornado moved northeast across southern Bibb County, it weakened to EF2 intensity while crossing Alabama Highway 5 south of West Blocton. According to the NWS survey, several mobile homes and single‑family homes near County Road 26 suffered major damage or were destroyed, and thousands of trees were downed along this part of the path, before the tornado finally lifted just northeast of Marvel. This later stage maintained a damaging but less intense character compared with the EF3 segments near Sawyerville and Eoline. 

The NCEI Storm Events entry for the Hale County segment of the tornado lists property damage of 17 million USD, with zero crop damage recorded, along with the destruction or damage of numerous residences, one church, and extensive timber losses. Although NCEI does not provide a single dollar figure for the entire multi‑county track, the Hale County estimate and the qualitative descriptions of heavy damage in Greene and Bibb counties indicate that the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado had a substantial economic impact on the affected rural communities. 

## Casualties

Official sources attribute multiple fatalities and dozens of injuries to the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado. The NWS Birmingham event page and its historic outbreak summary list a total of 7 fatalities and 50 injuries for the full track across Greene, Hale, and Bibb counties. An AL.com retrospective timeline similarly lists the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado as an EF3 event with 145 mph winds, affecting Greene, Hale, and Bibb counties with a 72.13‑mile track, and it assigns 7 deaths and 50 injuries to this tornado. 

By contrast, the NCEI Storm Events database entry for Event ID 314742, which covers only the Hale County portion of the track, lists 6 direct deaths and 40 direct injuries. The NWS and NCEI narratives indicate that these fatalities and injuries in Hale County occurred primarily in and around Sawyerville, Harper Hill, and Ingram, where extensive structural damage to mobile homes, single‑family houses, and a church accompanied the tornado’s EF3 phase. The difference between the Hale County segment figures and the full‑track totals reflects NCEI’s practice of reporting county‑segmented events, while NWS Birmingham aggregates casualties for the entire multi‑county Sawyerville–Eoline tornado. 

The NWS survey further notes that in the Eoline area of Bibb County, one fatality occurred in a vehicle near the destroyed Eoline Fire Department and that at least ten injuries were recorded in that segment of the path. Taken together, these reports indicate that fatal and non‑fatal injuries were distributed along the track, with concentrations in heavily damaged residential areas in both Hale and Bibb counties. 

## Warnings, emergency response, and immediate aftermath

NWS Birmingham reports that tornado warnings were in effect for Greene, Hale, and Bibb counties from 4:50 p.m. until 7:45 p.m. on April 27, 2011, covering the period during which the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado moved across the area. These warnings were issued as part of a broader sequence of watches and warnings associated with the afternoon and evening supercell thunderstorms that produced multiple tornadoes in central Alabama that day. 

The detailed NWS damage survey describes post‑storm inspection of multiple tracks across Greene, Hale, and Bibb counties, noting that meteorologists and survey teams documented consistent evidence of a strong, long‑tracked tornado along the route from near Tishabee through Sawyerville and Eoline to near Marvel. The survey notes the destruction of the Eoline Fire Department and another business, as well as damage to churches and numerous homes, indicating that local emergency services and community facilities were directly affected by the tornado. However, available sources focus primarily on meteorological and damage assessment aspects, and they provide limited detail on the organization of search‑and‑rescue operations or longer‑term relief efforts specific to this tornado. 

## Place in the 2011 Super Outbreak

In the context of the April 25–28, 2011 Super Outbreak, the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado is classified in NOAA‑linked summaries as an Alabama EF3 tornado that occurred on April 27 among the outbreak’s strong and violent events. Tornado Talk’s overview lists a specific write‑up titled “Sawyerville–Eoline, AL EF3 Tornado – April 27, 2011,” indicating that this tornado is treated as a distinct long‑track event within broader analyses of the outbreak. 

NOAA and NWS summaries describe the April 27 outbreak in Alabama as part of a historic tornado day that produced 316 fatalities across the Southeast, including 234 in Alabama, more than 2,400 injuries, and over 4.2 billion USD in damage. The same summaries state that during the 24‑hour period ending at 12:00 UTC on April 28, the number of tornadoes exceeded the previous 24‑hour record set during the April 3–4, 1974 Super Outbreak, and they characterize the April 27–28 event as the deadliest U.S. tornado outbreak since the March 18, 1925 Tri‑State tornado. Within this framework, the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado is one of several deadly tornadoes that struck Alabama on April 27, alongside higher‑rated events such as the Hackleburg EF5 and the Tuscaloosa–Birmingham EF4, but it remains notable as a long‑tracked EF3 that caused seven deaths and extensive damage in smaller communities and rural areas. 

## Notes on data sources and discrepancies

Different official sources provide varying quantitative figures for the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado because of differing reporting conventions. NWS Birmingham’s event page and historic outbreak table treat the tornado as a single, continuous track across Greene, Hale, and Bibb counties, listing an EF3 rating, a path length of 72.13 miles, a maximum width of 1,760 yards, and casualty totals of 7 fatalities and 50 injuries for the overall event. In contrast, the NCEI Storm Events database records a Hale County segment (Event ID 314742) with an EF3 rating, a 25.18‑mile segment length, the same 1,760‑yard maximum width, and 6 direct deaths and 40 direct injuries, along with 17 million USD in property damage for that county. The coexistence of these figures reflects NCEI’s county‑segmented cataloguing compared with NWS Birmingham’s whole‑track reporting, and both sets of values are cited in this article where relevant.

**_![Image 3](https://www.weather.gov/images/bmx/significant\_events/2011/042711/test2.jpg)_** **NEW: [Visit our April 27, 2011 in Alabama Webpage on the NOAA GeoPlatform](https://04272011-noaa.hub.arcgis.com/)** **Event Summary for Central Alabama** **As part of a system which wreaked havoc across the eastern half of the United States (April 25-28),the following is an account of the tornado outbreak of April 27th, 2011, in Central Alabama.** **National Weather Service meteorologists completed the assessment of storm damage from this tragically historic day of tornadic activity and severe weather across Central Alabama on Wednesday, April 27th. Nationally recognized storm damage experts assisted us in examining the locations of the most extreme damage to ensure we provided the most accurate assessment of this event as possible.** **In total, there were 29 confirmed tornadoes in Central Alabama on this day, and 62 confirmed tornadoes across the State of Alabama.** **Click on the numbered boxes on the map below to view more detailed information about each tornado track.** ![Image 4](https://www.weather.gov/images/bmx/GIS/042711_StatewideMap.jpg) **The tornado damage swaths as depicted in the image above, and on the individual tornado links, are an estimate of the damage widths along the track. In other words, the track width may not represent the actual damage in all locations, as we interpolate the values between actual surveyed damage points. These maps are soley for the purpose of showing the general track of each tornado. Remember, tornadoes do not always move in straight lines, and the intensity does not remain constant. It is also possible to have other thunderstorm wind-related damage in close proximity to the tornado tracks from such features as inflow and rear flank downdrafts, which can produce tornado-like damage. For a satellite image of the tornado tracks, [click here.](https://www.weather.gov/bmx/event_04272011satellite)** **For comprehensive GIS information, including ESRI Shapefiles and Google Earth KMZ files of tornado paths, storm survey points, and tracks of all 62 tornadoes, click on the link below:** [**![Image 5](https://www.weather.gov/images/bmx/GIS/esri.JPG)**](https://www.weather.gov/bmx/event_04272011gis)[![Image 6](https://www.weather.gov/images/bmx/GIS/KML.jpeg)](https://www.weather.gov/bmx/event_04272011gis) **[Pertinent Geographic Information Systems (GIS) Data from the April 27th, 2011 Outbreak](https://www.weather.gov/bmx/event_04272011gis)** **Important Note:The Shapefiles and KMLs are _experimental_ data.** **To tell the story of April 27, 2011, one has to recognize that there were two distinct waves of widespread severe weather in Central Alabama. The first wave of severe storms moved through during the early morning hours across northern portions of Central Alabama in the form of a Quasi-Linear Covective System (QLCS). This intense line of thunderstorms produced not only[widespread damaging straight line winds](https://www.weather.gov/bmx/event_04272011amstraightline) in the areas of Moody, Pell City and Riverside, but numerous strong tornadoes. April 25th-28th was one of the largest super-tornado outbreaks in US history.** **- There were 29 confirmed tornadoes in Central Alabama on April 27th. 62 tornadoes occurred across the state.** **- The combined tornado damage path length in Central Alabama was 691.02 miles.** **- Sixteen of the tornadoes had damage path lengths over 10 miles long.** **- Eight of the tornadoes had damage path lengths over 25 miles long.** **- Eight tornadoes either started or ended outside Central Alabama.** **- There were at least 1998 injuries reported and 240 people lost their lives.** **- [Tornado Watch 225](http://www.spc.noaa.gov/products/watch/2011/ww0225.html) was in effect from 226 am CDT until 8 am CDT.** **- [Tornado Watch 230](http://www.spc.noaa.gov/products/watch/2011/ww0230.html) was in effect from 812 am CDT until 2 pm CDT.** **- [PDS Tornado Watch 235](http://www.spc.noaa.gov/products/watch/2011/ww0235.html) was in effect from 145 pm CDT until 10 pm CDT.** **- [PDS Tornado Watch # Overview of the April 25-28, 2011 Super Outbreak

#### Published by [**Jen Narramore**](https://www.tornadotalk.com/author/admin/ "Jen Narramore") on April 27, 2021 April 23, 2026

[![Image 3](https://www.tornadotalk.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/04/Dbylm6xU8AA_-HR-1024x787.jpg)](https://www.tornadotalk.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/04/Dbylm6xU8AA_-HR.jpg)

Summary map from the April 25-28, 2011 Super Outbreak via U.S. Tornadoes.

368 Confirmed Tornadoes

4 Rated EF5. 11 Rated EF4. 21 Rated EF3.

224 Tornadoes on April 27. Most ever in a 24-hour period.

324 Fatalities. Over 3100 Injuries.

Estimated $12 Billion In Damage.

“The individual tornado paths from the April 25-28, 2011, Super Outbreak added up to an almost unfathomable 3,200 path miles, by far the greatest of any U.S. outbreak. This total path was over 600 miles longer than the April 3-4, 1974, Super Outbreak.” – Dr. Greg Forbes

_**Sources:**_

[On This Day: 2011 Tornado Super Outbreak | News | National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI)](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/news/2011-tornado-super-outbreak)

[2011 Super Outbreak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak)

[April 2011 Tornado Super Outbreak: 17 Things That Shocked Us Most | The Weather Channel – Articles from The Weather Channel | weather.com](https://weather.com/storms/tornado/news/2016-04-23-april-2011-superoutbreak-tornadoes#:~:text=The%20individual%20tornado%20paths%20from%20the%20April%2025-28%2C,longer%20than%20the%20April%203-4%2C%201974%2C%20Super%20Outbreak)

[U.S. Tornadoes](https://twitter.com/USTornadoes/status/989848612594208768?s=20)

A photo of the tornado near Houston, MS around this time. Image from Linda Griffin at the Chickasaw Emergency Management.

**_Sawyerville-Eoline (Greene,Hale and Bibb Counties)EF-3 Tornado April 27, 2011_** **Rating: [(_Click for EF Scale_)](https://www.weather.gov/bmx/enhancedfujitascale)****EF-3** **Estimated Maximum Wind:****145 mph** **Injuries/Fatalities:******50 Injuries /7 Fatalities**** **Damage Path Length:****72.13 miles** **Maximum Path Width:****1760 yards (1 mile)** **Approximate Start Point/Time:********32.6152/-88.0543 at 530 pm****** **Approximate End Point/Time:**************33.1524/-86.9898 at 655 pm************ **National Weather Service meteorologists surveyed multiple tracks across Greene, Hale and Bibb Counties. It has been determined that the damage was consistent with a strong tornado. The tornado touched down in far southwest Greene County near the Tombigbee River just West of Tishabee on County Road 69 near Head Drive, and headed northeast across rural Greene County north of Forkland. At least 4 mobile homes, 3 outbuildings, and 2 churches were damaged or destroyed along with numerous trees. Two minor injuries were noted in Greene County. The track started as an EF-1 but increased to an EF-2 rating while in Greene County.** **The tornado crossed the Black Warrior River and into Hale County west of Sawyerville. The tornado crossed AL Route 14, just north of Sawyerville, where it intensifyed to an EF-3 rating with winds of 145 mph. As the tornado continued northeast, it crossed CR 18, CR 21, AL Hwy 69 south of Harper Hill, and CR 29 east of Ingram. Extensive structural damage was noted in the these locations, which resulted in at least 40 injuries and 6 fatalities. Numerous mobile homes and single family homes and one church were damaged or destroyed. Thousands of trees were knocked down. The tornado moved into the Talladega National Forest near Ingram, where it caused significant tree damage to the Bibb County line.** **The tornado tracked northeastward where it caused significant tree damage in the national forest. The tornado moved through Eoline and caused significant structural damage consistent with an EF-3 rating and winds of 145 mph. Numerous mobile homes and single family homes sustained minor to major damage. A dozen mobile homes and single family homes were destroyed. In addition, the Eoline Fire Dept and another business were destroyed. One fatality occurred in a vehicle near the fire dept. At least 10 other injuries were noted. The tornado continued northeast and crossed AL Hwy 5, south of West Blocton where it weakened slightly to an EF-2 with winds of 125 mph. Several mobile homes and single family homes sustained major damage or were destroyed near CR 26. Along the path, thousands of trees were downed. The tornado continued to weaken and lifted just northeast of Marvel.** **Tornado Warnings were in effect for Greene, Hale and Bibb Counties from 450 pm until 745 pm.** **Radar Data** [![Image 3: Radar Image](https://www.weather.gov/images/bmx/significant_events/2011/042711/sawyerville/r2255.gif)](https://www.weather.gov/images/bmx/significant_events/2011/042711/sawyerville/r2255.gif)[![Image 4: Radar Image](https://www.weather.gov/images/bmx/significant_events/2011/042711/sawyerville/v2255.gif)](https://www.weather.gov/images/bmx/significant_events/2011/042711/sawyerville/v2255.gif) **This is an image of the 0.5 degree reflectivity data from KBMX at 555 pm as the circulation was over Sawyerville. Click to enlarge.****This is an image of the 0.5 degree storm relative velocity (SRM) data from KBMX at 555 pm as the circulation was over Sawyerville. Click to enlarge.** **Storm Damage Images** [![Image 5: Storm Damage Image](https://www.weather.gov/images/bmx/significant_events/2011/042711/sawyerville/1.JPG)](https://www.weather.gov/images/bmx/significant_events/2011/042711/sawyerville/1.JPG) **Eoline Volunteer Fire Dept Destroyed**[![Image 6: Storm Damage Image](https://www.weather.gov/images/bmx/significant_events/2011/042711/sawyerville/2.JPG)](https://www.weather.gov/images/bmx/significant_events/2011/042711/sawyerville/2.JPG) **Trees Snapped Off** [![Image 7: Storm Damage Image](https://www.weather.gov/images/bmx/significant_events/2011/042711/sawyerville/3.JPG)](https://www.weather.gov/images/bmx/significant_events/2011/042711/sawyerville/3.JPG) **Demolished Debris north of Water Oak**[![Image 8: Storm Damage Info](https://www.weather.gov/images/bmx/significant_events/2011/042711/sawyerville/4.JPG)](https://www.weather.gov/images/bmx/significant_events/2011/042711/sawyerville/4.JPG) **Mobile Home Destroyed in Hale Co.** [![Image 9: Storm Damage Image](https://www.weather.gov/images/bmx/significant_events/2011/042711/sawyerville/5.JPG)](https://www.weather.gov/images/bmx/significant_events/2011/042711/sawyerville/5.JPG) **Home Demolished near Tishabee in Greene Co**[![Image 10: Storm Damage Image](https://www.weather.gov/images/bmx/significant_events/2011/042711/sawyerville/7.JPG)](https://www.weather.gov/images/bmx/significant_events/2011/042711/sawyerville/7.JPG) **Roof Removed near Tishabee** [![Image 11: Storm Damage Image](https://www.weather.gov/images/bmx/significant_events/2011/042711/sawyerville/6.JPG)](https://www.weather.gov/images/bmx/significant_events/2011/042711/sawyerville/6.JPG) **Tree Debarked**

Episode Narrative**A powerful storm system crossed the Southeast United States on Wednesday, April 27, 2011, resulting in a large and deadly tornado outbreak. This epic event broke the record for number of tornadoes in a day for the state of Alabama, becoming the most significant tornado outbreak in the state���s history. 

 Central Alabama had two rounds of severe weather that day. During the early morning hours, a Quasi-Linear Convective System quickly moved across the northern half of the National Weather Service, Birmingham county warning area. Straight line winds of 90 mph (78kts) or greater and 11 tornadoes lead to widespread damage and power outages. During the afternoon, long-lived supercell thunderstorms produced long-track, strong and violent tornadoes. Destruction and loss of life across many towns and communities was devastating. 

 The hardest hit areas included Shottsville and Hackleburg, both in Marion County, where winds of 160 mph and 210 mph respectively, caused unimagineable damage. Cordova, in Walker County, was hit twice; by a tornado along the Quasi-Linear Convective System during the early morning hours and again in the afternoon by a long-track EF4 tornado. A long track tornado moved across the city of Tuscaloosa and the western suburbs of Birmingham, resulting in the complete destruction of whole neighborhoods and numerous injuries and fatalities in those heavily populated areas. The same parent supercell produced another violent tornado in east Central Alabama as it tracked across St. Clair and Calhoun Counties, resulting in additional fatalities and incredible damage to a number of neighborhoods. Another violent EF4 tornado tracked across portions of Elmore and Tallapoosa Counties, including Lake Martin, destroying numerous homes and a large section of a mobile home park. 

 Most of the violent tornadoes from this day were captured on video by a number of people, including storm spotters and chasers, as well as numerous television news crews and remotely controlled web-enabled video cameras. This allowed unprecedented coverage and viewing of this historic event in real time from people worldwide.**
Event Narrative**A tornado touched down in southwestern Greene County near Tishabee, and moved northeast through central Hale and Bibb Counties. The tornado then lifted near Marvel in far northeast Bibb County. The tornado crossed the Black Warrior River and into Hale County west of Sawyerville. The tornado crossed AL Route 14, just north of Sawyerville, intensifying to an EF3 rating with winds of 145 mph. As the tornado continued northeast, it crossed CR 18, CR 21, AL Hwy 69 south of Harper Hill, and CR 29 east of Ingram. Extensive structural damage was noted in the these locations, which resulted in at least 40 injuries and 6 fatalities. Numerous mobile homes and single family homes and one church were damaged or destroyed. Thousands of trees were knocked down. The tornado moved into the Talladega National Forest near Ingram, where it caused significant tree damage to the Bibb County line.**

## Details

*   **Corporate Authors:** [United States, National Weather Service,](http://repository.library.noaa.gov/gsearch?ref=docDetails&name_corporate=United%20States%2C%20National%20Weather%20Service%2C) 
*   **NOAA Program & Office:** [NWS (National Weather Service)](http://repository.library.noaa.gov/gsearch?ref=docDetails&sm_localcorpname=NWS%20%28National%20Weather%20Service%29) 
*   **Description:**  "On April 27, 2011, a series of devastating tornadoes struck the southeastern United States. This tornado event was one of the deadliest in the country since systematic tornado record keeping began in 1950. With 316 fatalities (31 in Mississippi, 234 in Alabama, 32 in Tennessee, 15 in Georgia, and 4 in Virginia), it ranks with the 1974 Super Tornado Outbreak and resulted in more deaths than the 1965 Palm Sunday Outbreak. In addition, there were more than 2,400 injuries. Damages from this outbreak totaled over $4.2 billion. The National Weather Service (NWS) formed a Service Assessment Team to evaluate its performance. To strengthen NWS relationships with other federal agencies involved with disaster work, for the first time this assessment had a co-leader from the Federal Emergency Management Agency. The team interviewed staff and reviewed products from the Storm Prediction Center (SPC), Weather Forecast Offices at Memphis and Morristown, TN, Jackson, MS, Huntsville and Birmingham, AL, and Peachtree City, GA. The team gathered feedback from partners and users of NWS products including media outlets, Emergency Managers at the state and local level, first responders, and the public. One of the team's tasks was to assess societal impacts of this event. This tornado outbreak was anticipated and forecast days in advance. The SPC began focusing on the affected area in its convective outlook products 5 days prior to the event. It continued emphasizing, refining, and enhancing the threat leading up to the event, ultimately issuing a high risk convective outlook on the morning of April 27 for a large portion of the impacted area. The Weather Forecast Offices (WFO) in the affected area prepared for severe weather operations and indicated the risk of severe weather and tornadoes as much as 5 days in advance. Hazardous Weather Outlooks, Web images, pre-recorded multimedia briefings, and webinars discussed the potential impacts. Emergency Managers and media staff interviewed indicated they were well prepared for the severe weather that occurred."--Page 1.

# 18 hours of horror: A look back at the tornadoes of April 27, 2011

*   Updated: Apr. 26, 2023, 10:25 p.m.
*   |Published: Apr. 27, 2022, 5:10 a.m.

![Image 1: April 27 tornado outbreak](https://www.al.com/resizer/v2/5J65NB336RB3ZMSQG77T625S6M.jpg?auth=ece084b10094bbcefabb0d1be811d7741ec155612024c98bb0d2fd4d22b99d68&width=1280&smart=true&quality=90)

Today marks 11 years since the tornado super outbreak of 2011 that killed 240 people in Alabama alone. Alabama wasn't the only state hit during the outbreak, which lasted from April 25th until the 28th, but it was hit the hardest.

*   Add us on Google

By 
*   [Leigh Morgan](https://www.al.com/staff/lmorgan/ "Leigh Morgan")

Eleven years ago today Alabama was in the midst of a weather nightmare -- the historic tornado outbreak of April 27, 2011.

Sixty-two tornadoes tracked across Alabama over an 18-hour period, carving out a damage path of more than 1,200 miles. At least 240 people died, and even more were injured.

Whole communities were destroyed. Some areas were hit more than once.

A subscription is required to read this story.

[Subscribe now to continue.](https://www.al.com/subscribe)

It was one of the largest tornado outbreaks in the U.S. to this day. The whole event spanned from April 25 until the 28th, but April 27th was the peak.

![Image 2: April 27, 2011, warnings](https://www.al.com/resizer/v2/GVHJI5DRRBHLZGNYOIKWNZI2PM.jpeg?auth=c20bf26870c42c860386256447ebde2da10fb324c1352e57da28ef415b15ef89&width=1280&smart=true&quality=90)

Alabama was hit with 62 tornadoes on April 27, 2011. Here are the warnings issued by the National Weather Service that day. At least 240 people were killed in Alabama.

Alabama was hit the hardest, according to NOAA. There were not one but two EF-5 monster tornadoes -- on one day.

The first was the Hackleburg tornado that had winds estimated at 210 mph. It had a path of devastation that was more than 132 miles long. Seventy-two people died in that storm, and 145 were injured.

The second had winds nearly as high, estimated at more than 200 mph, according to the National Weather Service. That storm is blamed for the deaths of 25 people in DeKalb County.

There were also a staggering seven -- seven -- EF-4s on that day, all of which formed within about five and a half hours.

### A 1-2-3 PUNCH

The April 27, 2011, outbreak came in three destructive waves that altogether lasted about 18 hours.

The first tornado touched down in Alabama at 4:01 a.m. on April 27. The last tornado of the day dissipated at 9:58 p.m.

### LONG-TRACK TORNADOES

![Image 3: April 27, 2011, tornado tracks](https://www.al.com/resizer/v2/RK5CEUWXSZD4ZGRURQTTJS3SOA.jpg?auth=eab1ebfe9c97ecf81abf40c0fe832284e311ff33fb8a1f156df816140778e404&width=1280&smart=true&quality=90)

Here are some of the tornado tracks from April 27, 2011. The longest track is No. 39 on the map and stretched for 123 miles.

The tornadoes of April 27 did not come and go but were of the dreaded long-track variety. Here are some of the longer tracks:

*   **123 miles:** EF-4, Cordova. Pickens, Tuscaloosa, Fayette, Cullman, Walker, Blount and Marshall counties. 13 deaths, 54 injuries.
*   **118.63 miles:** EF-5, Hackleburg. Marion, Franklin, Lawrence, Morgan, Limestone and Madison counties. 72 deaths, 145 injuries.
*   **80.68 miles:** EF-4, Tuscaloosa-Birmingham. Tuscaloosa, Jefferson counties, 65 deaths, 1,500 injuries.
*   **72.13 miles:** EF-3, Sawyerville-Eoline. Greene, Hale and Bibb counties, 7 deaths, 50 injuries.
*   **71.30 miles:** EF-4, Argo-Shoal Creek. Jefferson, St. Clair, Calhoun, Etowah and Cherokee counties. 22 deaths, 81 injuries.

### INCREDIBLE WINDS

![Image 4: 5th Anniversary of the April 27, 2011 Tornado Outbreak](https://www.al.com/resizer/v2/PREZ2F5NLJAFJBFQYPQ7AXVWQE.jpg?auth=3719a3d8ea5671d963144e5743a6fa9fb0bede8268443dc4f1079fa993b4c4cd&width=1280&smart=true&quality=90)

Total devastation on South Clay Street in Hackleburg a couple days after an EF-5 tornado on April 27, 2011. al.com

The two strongest tornadoes of April 27, 2011, had winds estimated at more than 200 mph:

*   **210 mph:** EF-5, Hackleburg tornado that affected Marion, Franklin, Lawrence, Morgan, Limestone and Madison counties.
*   **More than 200 mph**: EF-5, Rainsville tornado in DeKalb County.

Those two storms were two of four EF-5 tornadoes confirmed during the outbreak. There hasn’t been another EF-5 in the U.S. since 2013.

### 3 WAVES OF STORMS

#### MORNING WAVE

A violent squall line of storms moved through north and central Alabama early in the morning of April 27. The storms spawned a total of 19 tornadoes in north and central Alabama, including three EF-3 twisters, according to the National Weather Service. One person died and nearly 70 were hurt during this morning round of storms. The storms also knocked out the power to thousands, which was especially concerning with another more powerful round of storms expected later in the day.

**TIMELINE**

4:01 a.m., EF-1, 110 mph winds, Waterloo. Lauderdale County, 9.19-mile track.

4:16 a.m., EF-1, 100 mph winds, Dancy. Pickens County (started in Mississippi), 22.63-mile track.

4:19 a.m., EF-1, 90 mph, Smithsonia-Rhodesville. Lauderdale County, 1 injury, 1.8-mile track.

4:27 a.m., EF-2, 120 mph winds, Northern Reform. Pickens County, 14.36-mile track.

4:41 a.m., EF-3, 140 mph winds, Holman. Pickens and Tuscaloosa counties, 22-mile track.

Watch

5:03 a.m., EF-1, 100 mph winds, Berry. Fayette County, 4 injuries, 7.28-mile track.

5:17 a.m., EF-3, 155 mph winds, Coaling. Tuscaloosa and Jefferson counties, 20.26-mile track.

5:18 a.m., EF-3, 140 mph winds, Parrish-Cordova. Walker County, 40 injuries, 18.90-mile track (first of two tornadoes that would hit this area. The second one was even stronger).

5:48 a.m., EF-2, 120 mph winds, Hanceville-Holly Pond. Cullman County, 30.32-mile track.

5:50 a.m., EF-1, 100 mph winds, Altadena. Jefferson and Shelby counties, 3.39-mile track.

5:53 a.m., EF-2, 135 mph winds, Mountain Woods Lake. Jefferson and Blount counties, 3 injuries, 3.23-mile track.

5:54 a.m., EF-2, 120 mph winds, Cahaba Heights. Jefferson County, 20 injuries, 7.76-mile track.

Watch

6:12 a.m., EF-1, 105 mph winds, Liberty. Blount County, 10.68-mile path.

6:16 a.m., EF-2, 120 mph winds, Odenville. St. Clair County, 5 injuries, 3.84-mile track.

6:20 a.m., EF-1, 110 mph winds, Joppa-Lakeview. Cullman and Marshall counties, 11-mile track.

6:30 a.m., EF-2, 120 mph winds, Warrentown-Grove Oak. Marshall and DeKalb counties, 20-mile track.

6:58 a.m., EF-1, 110 mph winds, Shiloh-Section. Jackson County, 1 fatality, 27.85-mile track. (This morning tornado took a very similar track to an EF-4 tornado later in the afternoon, making it very difficult to distinguish which track was which.

7:10 a.m., EF-2, 120 mph winds, Henagar-Rosalie. DeKalb County, 5.75-mile track.

7:18 a.m., EF-1, 100 mph winds, Kaolin. DeKalb County, 4.05-mile track.

#### MIDDAY WAVE

A second wave of storms affected mainly north Alabama around midday on April 27. The National Weather Service said those storms also helped set the stage for what would happen later that afternoon. The second wave consisted of another squall line that caused wind damage and seven tornadoes in north Alabama.

**MIDDAY TIMELINE**

11:15 a.m., EF-0, 85 mph winds, Southwest Athens. Limestone County, 6.7-mile track.

11:20 a.m., EF-1, 105 mph winds, Decatur Industrial Park. Limestone and Morgan counties, 9-mile track.

11:23 a.m., EF-0, 70 mph winds, Tanner. Limestone County, 3.6-mile track.

11:30 a.m., EF-1, 110 mph winds, Monrovia-Deposit. Limestone and Madison counties, 25.3-mile track.

11:35 a.m., EF-1, 110 mph winds, Magnolia Springs-Harvest. Limestone and Madison counties, 3.2-mile track.

11:50 a.m., EF-1, 105 mph winds, Moores Mill-Winchester Road. Madison County, 7.6-mile track.

11:55 a.m., EF-0, 85 mph winds, Buckhorn High School. Madison County, 3.4-mile track.

#### EVENING WAVE

The worst was yet to come. A third wave of storms began on the afternoon of April 27th, what the National Weather Service calls the “March of the Supercells.” It began with a devastating EF-4 tornado that tracked through Cullman and also produced two deadly EF-5 monsters. Just 25 minutes later followed the horrific Hackleburg EF-5. An EF-4 tracked through Tuscaloosa and the northern suburbs of Birmingham just a short time later, resulting in multiple deaths. A second EF-5 struck eastern Alabama later that evening. The storms left “widespread and catastrophic damage” across parts of north and central Alabama.

**EVENING TIMELINE**

2:40 p.m., EF-4, 175 mph winds, Cullman. Cullman County, 6 deaths, 48 injuries, 46.88-mile path.

3:05 p.m., EF-5, 210 mph winds, Hackleburg. Marion, Franklin, Lawrence, Morgan, Limestone and Madison counties, 72 deaths, 145 injuries, 118.63-mile path.

3:40 p.m., EF-4, 170 mph winds, Cordova. Pickens, Tuscaloosa, Fayette, Cullman, Walker, Blount and Marshall counties, 13 deaths, 54 injuries, 123-mile path.

Watch

3:57 p.m., EF-3, 140 mph winds, Panola. Began in Mississippi and tracked through Sumter and Pickens counties, 2 injuries, 16.24-mile track.

4 p.m., EF-3, 160 mph winds, Shottsville. Began in Mississippi (where it was rated an EF-5) and tracked into Marion County, 7 deaths, 100 injuries, 18.48-mile track.

4:01 p.m., EF-4, 190 mph winds, Section-Flat Rock. Jackson County (continued into Georgia), 12 deaths, 27.76-mile track.

4:40 p.m., EF-1, 105 mph winds, Orvil Smith Road-Harvest. Madison County, 1.42-mile track.

4:43 p.m., EF-4, 190 mph winds, Tuscaloosa-Birmingham. Tuscaloosa, Jefferson counties, 65 deaths, 1,500 injuries, 80.68-mile path. According to the National Weather Service this tornado was produced by a supercell thunderstorm that began in Newton County, Miss., at 2:54 p.m., and finally dissipated in Macon County, N.C., at approximately 10:18 p.m. So, this supercell existed for about 7 hours and 24 minutes and traveled approximately 380 miles.

4:53 p.m., EF-1, 90 mph winds, Orrville-Monrovia. Limestone and Madison counties, 14.6-mile track.

5:05 p.m. EF-4, 180 mph winds, Bridgeport. Jackson County, 1 death, 20.24-mile track.

5:10 p.m., EF-3, 150 mph winds, Haleyville. Marion County, 25 injuries, 31.84-mile track.

5:30 p.m., EF-3, 145 mph winds, Sawyerville-Eoline. Greene, Hale and Bibb counties, 7 deaths, 50 injuries, 72.13-mile track. This tornado was on the ground for an hour and 25 minutes.

6:06 p.m., EF-3, 145 mph winds, Hubbertville. Fayette County, 7.96-mile track.

6:19 p.m., EF-5, estimated winds over 200 mph, Rainsville. DeKalb County, 25 deaths, 33.66-mile track. This same storm produced another EF-4 tornado in Ringgold, Ga., only 30 minutes later.

6:28 p.m., EF-4, 180 mph winds, Argo-Shoal Creek. Jefferson, St. Clair, Calhoun, Etowah and Cherokee counties, 22 deaths, 81 injuries, 71.30-mile track. This was the same parent storm that produced the deadly EF-4 tornado that tracked through parts of Tuscaloosa and Birmingham.

6:50 p.m., EF-1, 110 mph winds, Wateroak. Hale and Bibb counties, 8.62-mile track.

7:09 p.m., EF-0, 80 mph winds, West Point. Cullman County, 1.19-mile track.

7:10 p.m., EF-3, 120 mph winds, Cyril. Choctaw, Sumter, Marengo, Perry counties, 58-mile track. This tornado developed in Mississippi and strengthened to an EF-4 in that state, killing 7 people and injuring 17. There were no deaths in Alabama from the storm.

7:32 p.m., EF-1, 110 mph winds, Marvel. Bibb and Shelby counties, 5.41-mile track.

8:12 p.m., EF-4, 170 mph winds, Lake Martin. Elmore, Tallapoosa and Chambers counties, 7 deaths, 30 injuries, 44.18-mile track. This was the last of 11 violent tornadoes that affected Alabama on April 27th, although there were would be more twisters before the day was over.

8:15 p.m., EF-1, 105 mph winds, Vincent-Logan Martin. Shelby and Talladega counties, 8.59-mile track.

8:50 p.m., EF-1, Marion. Perry County, 4.24-mile track.

9:05 p.m., EF-2, 90 mph winds, Fort Payne-Fisher Crossroads. DeKalb County, 120 mph winds, 6.47-mile track.

9:19 p.m., EF-1, 110 mph winds, White Plains. Chambers County, 5.24-mile track.

9:29 p.m., EF-1, 90 mph winds, Finley Creek. Chambers County, 5.01-mile track.

## The March of the Supercells

**The third wave, which began with the Cullman EF-4 tornado, involved numerous supercell thunderstorms which produced deadly long-lived, strong to violent tornadoes across the northern two-thirds of Alabama. Widespread and catastrophic damage was sustained in several locations.**

## Cullman (EF-4)

[Open link](https://www.weather.gov/images/hun/stormsurveys/2011-04-27/radar/cullman_morgan_marshall/reflectivity_loop.gif)![Image 5: Dual-panel radar images showing precipitation intensity and wind velocity of the Cullman EF-4 Tornado on April 27, 2011.](https://storymaps.arcgis.com/stories/47cb7288a887417dbc3966b6ac5dba03)

[Open link](https://www.weather.gov/images/hun/stormsurveys/2011-04-27/radar/cullman_morgan_marshall/storm_relative_loop.gif)![Image 6: Dual-panel radar images showing precipitation intensity and wind velocity of the Cullman EF-4 Tornado on April 27, 2011.](https://storymaps.arcgis.com/stories/47cb7288a887417dbc3966b6ac5dba03)

**Time of Tornado: 2:40pm - 3:38pm Estimated Max Wind: 175 mph Max Width: 880 Yards (0.5 Mile) 6 Fatalities**

Developing on the north side of Lewis Smith Lake, a violent long-track tornado set on the path of destruction across Cullman, Morgan and Marshall Counties. This tornado downed trees and approached the city of Cullman after crossing Interstate 65. Some of the worst damage occurred just northeast of Highways 31 and 278 in Cullman, most notably with near total destruction of a church in downtown Cullman. The weather radio tower at this location was destroyed as well, wiping out vital life-saving information to the people in Cullman County. Destruction continued as the tornado moved northeast, debarking trees and completely destroying homes (some very well-built and dating back to the early 1900s). The tornado crossed into Morgan County near Hulaco, continuing northeast toward the Marshall County line. At this point, windspeeds were estimated at 190mph. The most severe damage from this tornado occurred along Highway 231 in Arab, particularly in the Ruth community, 3 miles north of Arab. A family of 9 was taking shelter in a home that was completely destroyed, killing 5 members of the family, including a baby girl. From here, homes were destroyed and trees were downed until the tornado crossed the Tennessee River, weakening considerably, and then lifting just northeast of Highway 431.

For additional information visit: [**https://www.weather.gov/hun/4272011_cullman_county**](https://www.weather.gov/hun/4272011_cullman_county)

## Hackleburg - Phil Campbell (EF-5)

[Open link](https://www.arcgis.com/sharing/rest/content/items/7fd6c743256a4dd7a456c40126428864/resources/Hackleburg_ref__1615320827293.gif)![Image 7: Dual-panel radar images showing precipitation intensity and wind velocity of the Hackleburg-Phil Campbell EF-5 Tornado on April 27, 2011.](https://storymaps.arcgis.com/stories/47cb7288a887417dbc3966b6ac5dba03)

[Open link](https://www.arcgis.com/sharing/rest/content/items/7fd6c743256a4dd7a456c40126428864/resources/Hackleburg_srm__1615320898763.gif)![Image 8: Dual-panel radar images showing precipitation intensity and wind velocity of the Hackleburg-Phil Campbell EF-5 Tornado on April 27, 2011.](https://storymaps.arcgis.com/stories/47cb7288a887417dbc3966b6ac5dba03)

**Time of Tornado: 3:05pm - 5:40pm Estimated Max Wind: 210 mph Max Width: 2200 yards (1.25 miles) 145 Injuries 72 Fatalities**

This tornado was on the ground for 132 miles, two hours and fifteen minutes. Thousands of trees were debarked, twisted, with nothing but trunks left. High tension power poles and trusses destroyed; concrete power poles snapped at the base. Hackleburg, Phil Campbell, Oak Grove, Tanner - devastated. In Hackleburg, the elementary, middle and high schools were all destroyed. The Wrangler plant too. A 25 foot section of pavement was sucked up in Phil Campbell and found 1/3 mile away. Along the path, mobile homes, vehicles, and cargo containers were mangled and tossed, some up to hundreds of yards away. Well-built homes were razed, leveled to the ground and foundations swept clean. Hundreds of buildings were destroyed and hundreds of others significantly damaged. The landscape was scarred and entire sections of forest mowed down. The tornado cycled several times, weakening and restrengthening again, before finally dissipating in Franklin County Tennessee.

## Cordova (EF-4)

[Open link](https://www.weather.gov/images/bmx/significant_events/2011/042711/cordovapm/radar_loop.gif)![Image 9: Dual-panel weather radar imagery from the Cordova EF-4 Tornado on April 27, 2011.](https://storymaps.arcgis.com/stories/47cb7288a887417dbc3966b6ac5dba03)

**Time of Tornado: 3:40pm - 5:56pm Estimated Max Wind: 170 mph Max Width: 1408 yards 54 Injuries 13 Fatalities**

For more than 127 miles and 2 hours, swaths of trees were splintered and debarked, mobile homes obliterated, houses leveled, and debris scattered across north Central Alabama. Touching down and moving parallel to damage from an early morning tornado, this tornado skirted southeastern Reform before strengthening southeast of Berry, destroying many homes. The tornado moved over mostly rural and forested land, briefly weakening as it crossed I-22. Taking aim at Cordova, still reeling from the morning EF-3, the tornado strengthened southwest of town and carved a swath of damage 0.5 miles wide through the central business district. Official city buildings, churches, businesses, and 20 percent of the homes in the area were destroyed. Strengthening to an EF-4 near Sipsey, large industrial and farm equipment were tossed aside like toys and numerous homes destroyed. The tornado straddled the Cullman – Blount county line, downing trees and damaging homes along Mulberry Fork. Additional homes were damaged, large vehicles tossed, and an industrial plant destroyed as the tornado rode along a wooded ridge line through central Blount County and southwest Marshall County. This supercell produced at least 4 violent tornadoes, from south central Mississippi to east Tennessee, including the EF-4 damage described here and EF-5 damage in northeast Alabama, near Rainsville.

For additional information visit:[](https://www.weather.gov/bmx/event_04272011cordova)[**https://www.weather.gov/bmx/event_04272011cordova**](http://www.weather.gov/bmx/event_04272011cordova)

## Section-Flat Rock (EF-4)

[Open link](https://www.weather.gov/images/hun/stormsurveys/2011-04-27/radar/jackson_dekalb_401_ef4/reflectivity_loop.gif)![Image 12: Dual-panel radar images showing precipitation intensity and wind velocity of the Section-Flat Rock EF-4 Tornado on April 27, 2011.](https://storymaps.arcgis.com/stories/47cb7288a887417dbc3966b6ac5dba03)

![Image 13](https://storymaps.arcgis.com/stories/47cb7288a887417dbc3966b6ac5dba03)

**Time of Tornado: 4:01pm - 4:36pm Estimated Max Wind: 190 mph Max Width: 1 mile 12 Fatalities**

Touching down in rural Jackson County, the tornado began its path of destruction about 3 miles northeast of Section. It rapidly intensified and began producing EF-3 to EF-4 damage within a matter of minutes, growing to a width of ½ to ¾ mile wide as it roared into Pisgah and Rosalie. Residents interviewed remarked that up to 3 tornadoes merged into one very large funnel, leveling homes and debarking trees in these locations. 6 people died at this point in the tornado path, 2 in Pisgah and 4 in the Higdon/Flat Rock communities. The tornado strengthened again and continued producing EF-4 damage in Flat Rock, growing larger than ¾ of a mile wide. Miraculously, a mother and 3 children taking shelter in a hallway were completely unharmed as the tornado disintegrated their home around them. Numerous farm animals perished at this particular farm, with most structures completely destroyed and their debris unidentifiable. The Shiloh community was affected next, and 5 people were killed as the tornado continued to obliterate trees and homes. A large number of farm animals also perished in this location, as the tornado crossed the Georgia line into Dade and later Walker Counties. Numerous injuries and several more fatalities occurred until the tornado lifted just south of the Tennessee state line in Northwestern Georgia.

Just northeast of the Stevenson Airport, the tornado produced EF-3 damage, twisting and flattening 24 high-tension truss towers. A violent tornado began to take shape in the Lakeview community northeast of Geraldine in rural Dekalb County. The tornado affected Fyffe, Rainsville, Sylvania, and eventually Cartersville. Trees were downed, some of them snapped at their bases, with the width of the tornado approximately 50 yards wide at the beginning of its track in Lakeview. As it moved northeast into Rainsville, the tornado strengthened significantly, growing to about ½ mile in width. Homes there were either completely destroyed or fully removed from their foundations with debris scattered for about 1 mile or more. Several people survived the tornado in their storm shelter here, with their mobile homes completely obliterated. Trees were debarked, asphalt was peeled from the ground, and significant scarring of the ground occurred. Still the tornado strengthened and grew larger as it moved northeast into the Cartersville community. Tornado width at this point was between ½ and ¾ mile wide, with complete destruction occurring of numerous homes in the area. From here, the tornado crossed the Georgia line into Dade County, lifting about 3 miles across the county line. ## Pin Hook - Faunsdale (EF-3 in AL)

[Open link](https://www.weather.gov/images/bmx/significant_events/2011/042711/pinhook/radar_loop.gif)![Image 27: Dual-panel radar images showing precipitation intensity and wind velocity of the Pin Hook-Faunsdale EF-3 Tornado on April 27, 2011.](https://storymaps.arcgis.com/stories/47cb7288a887417dbc3966b6ac5dba03)

**Time of Tornado: 7:10pm - 8:35pm Estimated Max Wind: 150 mph Max Width: 1000 yards 17 Injuries 7 Fatalities**

A violent tornado moved through southeast Mississippi and into Alabama, causing damage for over 125 miles. The tornado weakened slightly as it crossed the state line, but continued to cause extensive damage. More than a dozen homes and many farm buildings were significantly damaged or destroyed as it tracked through mostly rural farm land. Tree damage was considerable, as hundreds of trees were knocked down along the path, at times in a swath 350 yards wide. This tornado is the third to cross the Tombigbee River on this day. US Highway 43 stretches from Mobile to central Tennessee. This tornado is the eighth and final tornado to impact the US 43 corridor on this day.

For additional information visit: BMX: [](https://www.weather.gov/bmx/event_04272011pinhook)[**https://www.weather.gov/bmx/event_04272011pinhook**](https://www.weather.gov/bmx/event_04272011pinhook) MOB: [**https://www.weather.gov/mob/2011_April27_Tornado**](https://www.weather.gov/mob/2011_April27_Tornado)

## Lake Martin (EF-4)

[Open link](https://www.weather.gov/images/bmx/significant_events/2011/042711/lakemartin/radar_loop.gif)![Image 28: Dual-panel radar images showing precipitation intensity and wind velocity of the Lake Martin EF-4 Tornado on April 27, 2011.](https://storymaps.arcgis.com/stories/47cb7288a887417dbc3966b6ac5dba03)

**Time of Tornado: 8:12pm - 9:09pm Estimated Max Wind: 170 mph Max Width: 880 yards 30 Injuries 7 Fatalities**

Although supercells would produce weak tornadoes for a couple more hours, the tornado that devastated Lake Martin was the last of 11 violent (EF-4, EF-5) tornadoes to affect Alabama on this day. The tornado initially destroyed more than a dozen homes, businesses, and churches, with debris tossed up to 200 yards at some locations. The tornado strengthened as it approached Lake Martin from the southwest, increasing to one-half mile wide. Dozens of lakefront homes were significantly damaged or demolished as the tornado crossed the lake. Where the damage to homes was most severe, no walls were left standing above basement level. In wooded areas only debarked trunks remained. The tornado weakened east of the Lake, but continued to cause damage across more rural areas, finally lifting after being on the ground for almost an hour.

For additional information visit: [**https://www.weather.gov/bmx/event_04272011lakemartin**](https://www.weather.gov/bmx/event_04272011lakemartin)

## Vincent - Logan Martin (EF-1)

[Open link](https://www.weather.gov/images/bmx/significant_events/2011/042711/Vincent/radar_loop.gif)![Image 29: Dual-panel radar images showing precipitation intensity and wind velocity of the Vincent-Logan Martin EF-1 Tornado on April 27, 2011.](https://storymaps.arcgis.com/stories/47cb7288a887417dbc3966b6ac5dba03)

**Time of Tornado: 8:15pm - 8:24pm Estimated Max Wind: 105 mph Max Width: 200 yards**

The supercell that produced tornadoes near Wateroak and Marvel produced a third tornado that tracked parallel to the Coosa River and Logan Martin Lake, in mostly rural and forested land. Hundreds of trees were downed, which caused damage to homes in lakefront neighborhoods as the tornado was lifting.

For additional information visit: [**https://www.weather.gov/bmx/event_04272011vincent**](https://www.weather.gov/bmx/event_04272011vincent)

## Marion (EF-1)

[Open link](https://www.weather.gov/images/bmx/significant_events/2011/042711/Marion/radar_loop.gif)![Image 30: Dual-panel radar images showing precipitation intensity and wind velocity of the Marion EF-1 Tornado on April 27, 2011.](https://storymaps.arcgis.com/stories/47cb7288a887417dbc3966b6ac5dba03)

**Time of Tornado: 8:50pm - 8:53pm Estimated Max Wind: 90 mph Max Width: 100 yards**

A brief tornado caused damage along a 4 mile path south of Marion. Several outbuildings and a home were damaged. Additionally, many trees were knocked down along the short track. This tornado developed from the same supercell that produced a tornado and significant damage near Pin Hook and Faunsdale.

For additional information visit: [**https://www.weather.gov/bmx/event_04272011marion**](https://www.weather.gov/bmx/event_04272011marion)

## Fort Payne-Fisher Crossroads (EF-2)

[Open link](https://www.weather.gov/images/hun/stormsurveys/2011-04-27/radar/dekalb_sefortpayne/dekalb_sefortpayne_loop.gif)![Image 31: Dual-panel radar images showing precipitation intensity and wind velocity of the Fort Payne-Fisher Crossroads EF-2 Tornado on April 27, 2011.](https://storymaps.arcgis.com/stories/47cb7288a887417dbc3966b6ac5dba03)

**Time of Tornado: 9:05pm - 9:10pm Estimated Max Wind: 120 mph Max Width: 250 yards**

Damage from the tornado began as it touched down in southeastern Dekalb County along Dogtown Road, collapsing two small barns. Numerous trees were downed along the path, with the tornado strengthening significantly as it approached Highway 35. A barn was leveled and power poles were snapped off at their bases at this location, with damage to homes in the area as well. More trees were snapped and uprooted as the tornado tracked northeast, eventually lifting near Fisher Crossroads.

For additional information visit: [**https://www.weather.gov/hun/4272011_dekalb_dogtownroad**](https://www.weather.gov/hun/4272011_dekalb_dogtownroad)

## White Plains (EF-1)

[Open link](https://www.weather.gov/images/bmx/significant_events/2011/042711/WhitePlains/radar_loop.gif)![Image 32: Dual-panel radar images showing precipitation intensity and wind velocity of the White Plains EF-1 Tornado on April 27, 2011.](https://storymaps.arcgis.com/stories/47cb7288a887417dbc3966b6ac5dba03)

**Time of Tornado: 9:19pm - 9:28pm Estimated Max Wind: 110 mph Max Width: 150 yards**

The supercell that produced the tornado that devastated areas on Lake Martin, produced two additional, but weaker, tornadoes in Alabama. This one touched down near White Plains, downing numerous trees and causing damage to a home. As this tornado lifted, the storm re-cycled and produced another weak tornado that crossed Finley Creek.

For additional information visit: [**https://www.weather.gov/bmx/event_04272011whiteplains**](https://www.weather.gov/bmx/event_04272011whiteplains)

## Finley Creek (EF-1)

[Open link](https://www.weather.gov/images/bmx/significant_events/2011/042711/WhitePlains/radar_loop.gif)![Image 33: Dual-panel radar images showing precipitation intensity and wind velocity of the Finley Creek EF-1 Tornado on April 27, 2011.](https://storymaps.arcgis.com/stories/47cb7288a887417dbc3966b6ac5dba03)

**Time of Tornado: 9:29pm - 9:38pm Estimated Max Wind: 90 mph Max Width: 100 yards**

The violent tornado that crossed Lake Martin lifted, but the same supercell produced two additional, but weaker, tornadoes – one near White Plains and this one that crossed the Finley Creek area. Along its short path, many trees were knocked down and an outbuilding was damaged.

For additional information visit: [**https://www.weather.gov/bmx/event_04272011finleycreek**](https://www.weather.gov/bmx/event_04272011finleycreek)

## Verbena (EF-0)

[Open link](https://www.weather.gov/images/bmx/significant_events/2011/042711/Verbena/radar_loop.gif)![Image 34: Dual-panel radar images showing precipitation intensity and wind velocity of the Verbena EF-0 Tornado on April 27, 2011.](https://storymaps.arcgis.com/stories/47cb7288a887417dbc3966b6ac5dba03)

**Time of Tornado: 9:48pm - 9:50pm Estimated Max Wind: 80 mph Max Width: 50 yards**

The last tornado to affect Alabama on April 27, 2011 briefly touched down near Verbena, and occurred from the same supercell that produced the Pin Hook and Faunsdale tornado and the Marion tornado. Along its short path of less than 2 miles, many trees were knocked down and two homes received minor damage.

For additional information visit: [**https://www.weather.gov/bmx/event_04272011verbena**](https://www.weather.gov/bmx/event_04272011verbena)

**Epic Outbreak of Tornadoes Across the**

**Southeast on 27-28 April 2011 Impacts**

**Northeast Georgia and Western North Carolina**

![Image 4: Aerial view of EF-3 damage to large wood-frame homes on Meeting House Mtn Road at Lake Burton in Rabun County, Georgia, on 27 April 2011.](https://www.weather.gov/images/gsp/local_research/2011/EpicOutbreak/meeting_house_road2.jpg)

**The same supercell thunderstorm that produced the violent tornado that devastated Tuscaloosa, Alabama, tracked across north Georgia and into Rabun County, Georgia, around 11 pm on 27 April 2011. The supercell produced a tornado over Lake Burton that caused at least one fatality.**

_Author's Note: The following report has not been subjected to the scientific peer review process._

**1. Introduction**An epic tornado outbreak occurred across parts of the eastern United States 
during the afternoon and evening of Wednesday, 27 April 2011, and continued 
into the early morning hours of Thursday, 28 April 2011.  The number of 
tornadoes for the 24 hour period ending at 1200 UTC on 28 April 2011 
shattered the previous record set during the "Super Outbreak" of 3-4 April 
1974 (Fujita 1975).  The death toll was second only to the outbreak of 
18 March 1925, which included [the infamous "Tri-State Tornado"](https://www.crh.noaa.gov/pah/?n=1925tor) (Changnon 
_et al._ 1966).  The number of strong to violent tornadoes (EF3 intensity or 
greater on the [Enhanced Fujita Scale](http://www.spc.noaa.gov/efscale/)) over the southern Appalachian Mountains 
of North Carolina, Tennessee, and north Georgia (Table 1) was the most since 
[the Palm Sunday tornadoes of 1994](http://www.nws.noaa.gov/os/assessments/pdfs/palmsunday.pdf), and the third instance of multiple violent 
tornadoes in the same day since 1950.  The devastating tornadoes of 27 April 
2011 were part of a larger outbreak of severe weather, mainly across the 
Southeast, that spanned four days from 25 April to 29 April (Fig. 1).[Click here to read the official NWS Service Assessment](http://www.nws.noaa.gov/os/assessments/pdfs/historic_tornadoes.pdf)[Go here for a clickable map of event reviews from other NWS offices](https://www.srh.noaa.gov/hun/?n=hunsur_2011-04-27_main#other_cwas)[![Image 5: Table of strong to violent tornadoes over the southern Applachians of NC, TN, and GA](https://www.weather.gov/images/gsp/local_research/2011/EpicOutbreak/Table.png)](https://www.weather.gov/images/gsp/local_research/2011/EpicOutbreak/Table.png)**Table 1. F3/EF3 and F4/EF4 tornadoes in the southern Appalachian Mountains of North Carolina, Tennessee, and north Georgia since 1950. Click on image to enlarge.**
[![Image 6: Preliminary reports of large hail, damaging wind, and tornadoes for 25 April 2011](https://www.weather.gov/images/gsp/local_research/2011/EpicOutbreak/110425_rpts.png)](https://www.weather.gov/images/gsp/local_research/2011/EpicOutbreak/110425_rpts.png)[![Image 7: Preliminary reports of large hail, damaging wind, and tornadoes for 26 April 2011](https://www.weather.gov/images/gsp/local_research/2011/EpicOutbreak/110426_rpts.png)](https://www.weather.gov/images/gsp/local_research/2011/EpicOutbreak/110426_rpts.png)

[![Image 8: Preliminary reports of large hail, damaging wind, and tornadoes for 27 April 2011](https://www.weather.gov/images/gsp/local_research/2011/EpicOutbreak/110427_rpts.png)](https://www.weather.gov/images/gsp/local_research/2011/EpicOutbreak/110427_rpts.png)[![Image 9: Preliminary reports of large hail, damaging wind, and tornadoes for 28 April 2011](https://www.weather.gov/images/gsp/local_research/2011/EpicOutbreak/110428_rpts.png)](https://www.weather.gov/images/gsp/local_research/2011/EpicOutbreak/110428_rpts.png)

**Figure 1. Preliminary reports of tornadoes, large hail, and thunderstorm wind damage collected by the Storm Prediction Center from NWS local storm reports for the 24 hour period ending at 1200 UTC on 26 April 2011 (upper left), 27 April 2011 (upper right), 28 April 2011 (lower left), and 29 April 2011 (lower right). Click on images to enlarge.**As in the Super Outbreak, northeast Georgia and western North Carolina did not 
bear the brunt of the tornadic activity on 27-28 April 2011.  However, those 
locations were not entirely spared either.  In fact, the events of 27-28 April 
bore an eerie resemblance to the Super Outbreak over the western Carolinas and 
northeast Georgia (Figs. 2 and 3).  In both events, a supercell thunderstorm 
moved across north Georgia and produced tornadoes in extreme northeast Georgia.  
Furthermore, both events had two tornadoes reported over the northern foothills 
of North Carolina. At least two tornadoes briefly touched down in the mountains 
of North Carolina on 27 April, although several more tornadoes occurred in 
southwest North Carolina during the Super Outbreak.[Click here to view a map of tornado tracks on 27-28 April 2011](https://www.srh.noaa.gov/srh/ssd/mapping/)![Image 10: Tornado tracks for the April 1974 Super Outbreak](https://www.weather.gov/images/gsp/local_research/2011/EpicOutbreak/outbreakmapsmall.gif)**Figure 2. Tornado tracks during the "Super Outbreak" of 3-4 April 1974 (Fujita 1975). The 148 tornadoes documented during the outbreak are numbered sequentially in the figure.**[![Image 11: Track of tornadoes across the Southeast on 27 April 2011](https://www.weather.gov/images/gsp/local_research/2011/EpicOutbreak/SoutheastTornadoTracks.gif)](https://www.weather.gov/images/gsp/local_research/2011/EpicOutbreak/SoutheastTornadoTracks.gif)**Figure 3. Preliminary tornado tracks for 24-29 April 2011 across the southeastern United States. The tracks are color coded by maximum EF-scale rating as shown in the legend. Click on image to enlarge.**The events of 27-28 April 2011 were highly anticipated by the forecasters at 
the Storm Prediction Center (SPC) and at the Greenville - Spartanburg (GSP) 
Weather Forecast Office (WFO), even if the convective mode was not entirely
appreciated until the evening of 27 April.  The potential for severe 
thunderstorms was first mentioned by GSP in the Hazardous Weather Outlook 
issued in the afternoon of 23 April.  By that time, the SPC had already 
included the western part of the Carolinas in [the severe weather outlook for Day 5 (1200 UTC 27 April to 1200 UTC 28 April)](https://www.weather.gov/gsp/Day5Outlook_23April), which mentioned the possibility 
of isolated tornadoes.  [Every subsequent outlook issued by the SPC](https://www.weather.gov/gsp/Day4Outlook_24April) had part 
or all of the [GSP county warning area (CWA)](https://www.weather.gov/images/gsp/GSP_TopographicFinal_LowRes.png) in a severe weather risk area for 
that time period.  The expected threat gradually increased, with the potential 
for a tornado outbreak in the Tennessee Valley first mentioned in [the Day 3 outlook issued at 0730 UTC on 25 April](https://www.weather.gov/gsp/Day3Outlook_25April), and continued on [the Day 2 outlooks issued at 0600 UTC](https://www.weather.gov/gsp/Day2Outlook_26Apr_0600Z) and [1730 UTC on 26 April](https://www.weather.gov/gsp/Day2Outlook_26Apr_1730Z).  The threat culminated in a 
moderate risk over the western half of the CWA on [the Day 1 outlook issued at 0610 UTC on 27 April](https://www.weather.gov/gsp/Day1Outlook_27Apr_1200Z), with the significant tornado potential extending 
into the southern mountains of North Carolina, northeast Georgia, and the 
western tip of South Carolina.**2. Tornado Summary**Four distinct supercell thunderstorms moved across north Georgia and western 
North Carolina, producing at least five tornadoes within the GSP CWA during 
the late evening of 27 April 2011 and early morning hours of 28 April 2011 
(Fig. 4).  The first supercell moved across Cocke and Greene counties in 
Tennessee and produced [a brief and weak tornado northwest of Hot Springs (Madison County), North Carolina](https://www.weather.gov/gsp/NWMadisonTornado).  The second supercell was by far the most 
intense and quite possibly the most impressive storm of the entire outbreak.  
The supercell reached northeast Georgia in the late evening and produced a 
long-track significant tornado that began in northeast Lumpkin County.  [The tornado remained on the ground across northern White County, the northwest corner of Habersham County near Goshen Mountain, and then crossed Rabun County from Lake Burton to just northeast of Mountain City, where it lifted on the side of Oakey Mountain](https://www.weather.gov/gsp/LumpkinWhiteRabunTrack).  The damage along most of the track from Lumpkin 
to northwest Habersham counties was rated at EF2 on the Enhanced Fujita Scale.  
The damage at Lake Burton was rated at EF3 and caused one fatality and at 
least five injuries, making this tornado the strongest in the GSP CWA since 
the Dudley Shoals (Caldwell County), North Carolina, F4 tornado on 7 May 1998.  
It was also the first significant tornado to strike Rabun County since the Palm 
Sunday Outbreak on 27 March 1994.  The third supercell moved on a nearly 
identical path across Rabun County, Georgia, and across Macon County, North 
Carolina, where it produced [a brief, weak tornado in the Scaly Mountain community](https://www.weather.gov/gsp/ScalyMtTornado).  The fourth supercell moved along the Blue Ridge and then across the 
northern foothills of North Carolina, eventually producing tornadoes [southeast of Lenoir in Caldwell County, North Carolina](https://www.weather.gov/gsp/ErnCaldwellTornado), and [west of Taylorsville in Alexander County, North Carolina](https://www.weather.gov/gsp/EllendaleTornado).  The damage from both tornadoes was rated at 
EF1 intensity.[![Image 12: Tracks of tornadoes across northeast Georgia and western North Carolina on 27-28 April 2011](https://www.weather.gov/images/gsp/local_research/2011/EpicOutbreak/TornadoTracks.jpg)](https://www.weather.gov/images/gsp/local_research/2011/EpicOutbreak/TornadoTracks.jpg)**Figure 4. Click on image to enlarge.**All five tornadoes occurred with a Tornado Watch in effect.  The first tornado 
had no warning in effect, but the other four had a Tornado Warning.  The 
average initial lead time was 17.8 minutes and the average event lead time was 
22.6 minutes.**3. Synoptic and Pre-Storm Environment**The synoptic weather pattern was highly conducive to an outbreak of severe 
thunderstorms over the Southeast on 27-28 April.  A high amplitude upper trough 
at 500 mb was situated over the Plains at 1200 UTC on 27 April, with a short 
wave trough evident over Oklahoma and Texas (Fig. 5).  A mid-level jet streak 
of 80-90 kt was rounding the base of the trough over the southern Plains.  A 
similar arrangement was noted at 700 mb, with a 70 kt wind observation over 
north Texas (Fig. 6).  Water vapor satellite imagery showed evidence of the 
strong mid-level winds moving with the short wave as the area of relatively 
dry air over Texas, Louisiana, and southwest Mississippi (Fig. 7).  At 850 mb, 
a 50 kt low level jet over the area from Louisiana to Georgia advected warm, 
moist air northward from the Gulf of America (Fig. 8).  Morning upper air 
observations over the Southeast showed a capping inversion around 800-850 mb 
and steep mid-level lapse rates from the remnants of an elevated mixed layer.  
At the surface, a broad warm sector covered the entire Southeast and Carolinas 
ahead of a quasi-stationary front stretched across east Texas and Arkansas 
(Fig. 9).  The updated [Day 1 Convective Outlook issued at 1300 UTC](https://www.weather.gov/gsp/Day1Outlook_27Apr_1300Z) maintained 
the threat for severe thunderstorms and tornadoes over the western Carolinas
and northeast Georgia.[Click here to view a 25 frame loop of GOES-13 water vapor channel satellite imagery from 1145 UTC on 27 April to 1145 UTC on 28 April 2011.](https://www-md.weather.gov/gsp/EpicOutbreakWV)[![Image 13: 500 mb analysis at 1200 UTC on 27 April 2011](https://www.weather.gov/images/gsp/local_research/2011/EpicOutbreak/500_110427_12.gif)](https://www.weather.gov/images/gsp/local_research/2011/EpicOutbreak/500_110427_12.gif)**Figure 5. Click on image to enlarge.**[By 2200 UTC on 27 April, it was already clear that a remarkable event was well underway across the Southeast](https://www.weather.gov/gsp/PublicOutlook_2200Z) with [numerous tornadic supercells over parts of Alabama and Tennessee](https://www.weather.gov/images/gsp/loops/EpicOutbreakRegionalRefl/KGSP_RegionalRadar_27Apr2158Z.gif), although the western Carolinas and northeast 
Georgia had not been affected at that time.  At 0000 UTC on 28 April 2011, a 
short wave trough was analyzed at 500 mb from southern Missouri to the 
Arklatex Region, with a strong mid-level jet streak of at least 90 kt lifting 
out from the trough axis northeastward across the Tennessee Valley (Fig. 11).  
[Similar features were noted at 700 mb](https://www.weather.gov/images/gsp/local_research/2011/EpicOutbreak/700_110428_00.gif).  Meanwhile, a southerly low level jet 
of 40-60 kt was observed at 850 mb across Alabama and western Georgia to the 
Tennessee Valley (Fig. 12).  The upper air sounding taken at Peachtree City, 
Georgia (FFC), was representative of the environment immediately ahead of [the supercells moving northeast from Alabama](https://www.weather.gov/images/gsp/loops/EpicOutbreakRegionalRefl/KGSP_RegionalRadar_27Apr2358Z.gif) (Fig. 13).  The sounding was 
moderately buoyant with a convective available potential energy (CAPE) of 
2100 J kg-1 but with a relatively dry boundary layer as compared to locations 
to the west.  The surface dewpoint was only 62 oF which resulted in a lifting 
condensation level (LCL) of greater than 1200 m and limited CAPE below about 
600 mb.  Storm relative helicity (SRH) of greater than 250 m2s-2 in the surface 
to 1 km layer and around 400 m2s-2 in the surface to 3 km layer was highly 
supportive of the development and maintenance of supercell thunderstorms.  The 
surface front moved east as a cold front and stretched from south to north 
across Mississippi to western Tennessee and western Kentucky (Fig. 14).  
[Surface observations showed two plumes of moisture](https://www.weather.gov/images/gsp/local_research/2011/EpicOutbreak/2011042800_metars_clt.gif): one along the Georgia coast 
and the eastern half of the Carolinas, and the other from the Gulf Coast 
northward across Alabama.  In between the two plumes, a relatively dry patch 
of air was located from central and northeast Georgia to Upstate South Carolina 
and the foothills of North Carolina.  Again, no change was made to the severe 
weather risk for the western Carolinas and northeast Georgia when [the Day 1 Convective Outlook was updated at 0050 UTC on 28 April](https://www.weather.gov/gsp/Day1Outlook_28Apr_0100Z).[![Image 19: 500 mb analysis at 0000 UTC on 28 April 2011](https://www.weather.gov/images/gsp/local_research/2011/EpicOutbreak/500_110428_00.gif)](https://www.weather.gov/images/gsp/local_research/2011/EpicOutbreak/500_110428_00.gif)**Figure 11. potential impact on western North Carolina and northeast Georgia (Fig. 18).

The NW Madison County Tornado**The first supercell moved northeast across the eastern-most counties of 
Tennessee in the early part of the evening, then reorganized over Cocke 
County around 0230 UTC on 28 April.  The center of a broad mesocyclone was 
on track to move west of the western tip of Madison County, North Carolina, 
to the northwest of Hot Springs.  Two brief tornadoes touched down in southern 
Cocke County:  near Hartford at 0230 UTC, and near Del Rio at 0238 UTC.  Both 
tornadoes were unknown at the time, but WFO Morristown (KMRX) had a Tornado 
Warning for that part of Cocke County adjacent to Madison County valid until 
0300 UTC.  While the main mesocyclone strengthened as it moved past Madison 
County, a smaller low-level circulation developed by 0242 UTC about three 
miles north of Round Mountain along what appeared to be a rear flank 
downdraft (Fig. 19).  This weaker feature moved across the extreme 
northwestern part of Madison County between 0242 UTC and 0251 UTC.  Maximum 
rotational shear quickly climbed above 0.020 s-1 and peaked at 0.031 s-1 over 
northwest Madison County at 0247 UTC on the 0.5 degree scan from the KMRX 
radar (Fig. 20).  [A tornado touched down four miles northwest of Hot Springs, and just one-half mile east of the state line, at approximately 0247 UTC](https://www.weather.gov/gsp/EpicOutbreakNWMadisonTornado).  
The tornado felled and snapped numerous trees in multiple directions and 
damaged three outbuildings along a path 50 yards wide and 100 yards long.  
The damage was rated at EF0 on the Enhanced Fujita Scale.  An additional 
swath of straight line wind damage was noted to the south of the tornado track.[Click here to view a 10 frame loop of reflectivity on the 0.5 degree scan from the KMRX radar from 0215 UTC to 0256 UTC on 28 April 2011.](https://www.weather.gov/gsp/EpicOutbreakKMRXref)[Click here to view an 8 frame loop of storm relative motion on the 0.5 degree scan from the KMRX radar from 0215 UTC to 0256 UTC on 28 April 2011.](https://www.weather.gov/gsp/EpicOutbreakKMRXsrm)[![Image 27: KMRX 0.5 degree base reflectivity and storm relative motion at 0242 UTC 28 April 2011](https://www.weather.gov/images/gsp/local_research/2011/EpicOutbreak/KMRX_2panel0242.gif)](https://www.weather.gov/images/gsp/local_research/2011/EpicOutbreak/KMRX_2panel0242.gif)**Figure 19. broad with a diameter greater than 3.0 nm on all scans.  The rotational 
velocity was in the 35 kt to 40 kt range at a distance of greater than 70 nm, 
which placed the circulation in the "moderate mesocyclone" area of the 
mesocyclone recognition nomogram.  However, the broad diameter resulted in 
relatively weak shear, which placed the storm in the "minimal mesocyclone"
